But the three-word program still reuses each state 3.20 times, not the predicted under-1.5. The reason is structural: an input sharing its subtrahend and outer count with another converges onto the same inner-loop suffix whatever its starting value, so a subtractive loop has heavy suffix convergence BY CONSTRUCTION. WIDENING THE STATE DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY DESTROY SHARING. Convergence is a property of the map, not of the state count, and a tabulator exploits convergence rather than smallness. Reuse fell 3.3x, which is real, and nowhere near enough to call the sharing dead.

predictions.claim: AG4 overstated: extra state multiplies only the attacker cost while a work factor multiplies both, so the ratio improves only with state
predictions.note: Held exactly, and it corrects AG4. Widening the state by one word multiplies the attacker's bill by 729 and leaves the honest cost at 1,150 steps, untouched. Moving to a device-level tick multiplies BOTH by 5,400 -- the honest party pays 6,210,000 node-updates for the same run. SO THE RATIO GAINS 729x FROM STATE AND EXACTLY 1x FROM THE WORK FACTOR. AG4 called the work factor "worth slightly more than one word of state", which treats the two as one currency; on the asymmetry it is worth nothing at all. What it buys is ABSOLUTE infeasibility -- turning a cheap attack into an expensive one in wall-clock terms -- which is real, is what a KDF is for, and is a different claim. AG4 never measured the honest side, which is the only place the difference shows.

predictions.claim: tabulating costs more than 10^11 state-evaluations against fewer than 300 honest steps, a ratio above 10^8, identical at either tick level
predictions.note: FAILED on both magnitudes and held on its structural point. The control space is (w, b, c) = 729^3 = 387,420,489, not the 10^11 predicted -- that figure was 729^4, which counts a fourth word this program does not have, since its step counter never gates a branch. And one honest run costs 1,150 steps rather than under 300, because the loop is genuinely long. The margin is therefore 3.37 x 10^5, not above 10^8: real, and three orders short of the claim. The clause that held is the one AH3 predicts: the margin is IDENTICAL under an instruction tick and a device tick, because the work factor cancels out of a ratio exactly. Quote the margin as a ratio and it is a statement about the state space alone; quote it in seconds and the work factor is the whole story. Both are true and they answer different questions.

prediction_sets.subject: The n+1 arity ladder, and the feedback functions that make a trajectory graph tree-like

predictions.claim: the Ladder's history operator replicates past the nine steps it was checked over, with no genesis exception
predictions.note: H(prev) = SUM prev + [prev != empty] reproduces Fibonacci with two zeros at the front for all 40 terms checked, against the 9 the Ladder itself verified, and there is no special case at the genesis -- which is the operator's whole claim to being more fundamental than the two-term recurrence. Three of the four competing rules fail exactly where the Ladder says: cur+last first at step 1, sum(prev) wrong at 8 of 9, sum(prev)+1 first at step 0. The fourth disagrees -- my reconstruction of "cur + len(prev)" first fails at step 2 where the Ladder records 6 -- and that is a fact about reading a four-word label, not about its result. The definitions were left as read rather than tuned until they agreed, which would be fitting the instrument to the answer.

predictions.claim: the arity ladder cubes at every rung, and passes the width ladder at n = 3
predictions.note: Exact at every rung: 27, 19,683, 7,625,597,484,987, then a 39-digit number, each the cube of the last because 3^(3^(n+1)) = (3^(3^n))^3. This is a different growth law from the one this project has been using. AD4's width ladder MULTIPLIES by 729 per live word; the arity ladder CUBES. Arity passes width at n = 3 and by n = 4 they are not in the same range -- 39 digits against 15. Adding an input is not a bigger version of adding a word, it is a different operation.
predictions.at_risk: NOT AT RISK: "each rung is exactly the CUBE of the last, since 3^(3^(n+1)) = (3^(3^n))^3", with 27, 19,683 and 7,625,597,484,987 all given.

predictions.claim: the reversible fraction is (2/9)^(3^(n-1)), and it reproduces AB1's swept 1.097% from a formula
predictions.note: A function is reversible in its leading argument exactly when each of its 3^(n-1) columns is a bijection of three values, so the count is 6^(3^(n-1)) and the fraction (2/9)^(3^(n-1)). AB1 measured 216 of 19,683 by sweeping every table one at a time; the formula gives the same figure to four significant figures without a sweep, and 216 is exactly 6^3. SO AB1 WAS ONE RUNG OF A LADDER NOBODY HAD WRITTEN DOWN. The fraction collapses fast -- 22.22%, 1.097%, then 0.000132% -- which is the arity version of the scarcity M1 found at fixed width.
predictions.at_risk: NOT AT RISK: The closed form 6^(3^(n-1)) and the fraction (2/9)^(3^(n-1)) are stated and evaluated at 22.22%, 1.097% and 0.000132% -- and the 1.097% was already AB1's measurement.
predictions.argument: A function is reversible in its leading argument exactly when each of its 3^(n-1) columns is a bijection of three values. So the count is 6^(3^(n-1)) and the fraction (2/9)^(3^(n-1)), for every n — a closed form, not a fit.

predictions.claim: a leading-argument-reversible feedback function makes the shift-register state map a bijection, so no two trajectories ever merge
predictions.note: HELD, and it answers what AH2 left open. Taking an n-input function as shift-register feedback -- state (x1..xn), next (x2..xn, f(x1..xn)) -- a leading-argument-reversible f makes the state map a BIJECTION: maximum in-degree exactly 1, zero unreachable states, every one of the 531,441 states with in-degree 1. Nothing merges, so a tabulator's reuse is exactly 1.00 against AH2's 3.20 and hailstone's 10.43, and there is nothing to amortise. The non-reversible comparison is worse than predicted rather than better: tritwise MIN gives a maximum in-degree of 729 and leaves 91.22% of the state space UNREACHABLE, against a predicted quarter. So AB1's 216 tables are not a curiosity. THEY ARE EXACTLY THE FEEDBACK FUNCTIONS THAT MAKE THE FOURTH FACTOR COME OUT RIGHT, and this project measured them four sets before it knew what they were for.
predictions.argument: With state (x1..xn) and next (x2..xn, f(x1..xn)), a leading-argument-reversible f makes the state map injective: two states with the same successor would need the same tail and the same f-value, forcing them equal. Holds for every n.

prediction_sets.subject: What self-reference buys, and what actually buys the property it is asked for

predictions.claim: the ladder step carried in two words is injective, with in-degree exactly 1 everywhere, because every component is ADD
predictions.note: Maximum in-degree 1, zero unreachable, over all 531,441 (sum, lag) states -- AI4's bijection criterion met with NO special feedback table. The inverse is explicit rather than abstract: given (sum+lag, sum+1), recover sum = second - 1 and lag = first - sum, and it recovered all five probes including the wrapping corner (364,-364). THE PROPERTY IS REVERSIBILITY, NOT SELF-REFERENCE, and not memory either: a FORGETFUL two-word carry has it exactly as much as an append-only history would, because every component is ADD and AB2 measured ADD at zero bits erased. AI4 had to search 19,683 tables to find 216 that work; this needs nothing but addition.
predictions.argument: Every component is ADD, which erases nothing, and the inverse is explicit: from (sum+lag, sum+1) recover sum = second - 1 and lag = first - sum. An explicit inverse is a proof of injectivity, not evidence of it.

predictions.claim: H as a value map erases more than 3 bits, so the reversibility lives in the state rather than in what is emitted
predictions.note: Eighty-one histories of length four collapse onto nine outputs, erasing 3.5944 bits by the AB measure. The state map is a bijection and the emitted value is a nine-to-one channel, at the same time and without contradiction, because they are different maps. Anyone reading only the number H produces is reading an erasing channel however well-behaved the state carrying it happens to be -- which is the distinction AB2 already drew between the accumulator reading and the pair reading, arriving here from a completely different direction.

predictions.claim: the operator runs in the machine that would price it, and the implementation erases even though the mathematics does not
predictions.note: programs/ladder.tasm reproduces the ladder exactly against an independent implementation, so the operator is now self-hosting in the weak sense -- expressible in the language its own ladder produces. It costs 152 instructions for nine terms and erases 6.2564 bits per instruction, which is the second-highest figure in the corpus after fold. SELF-HOSTING DOES NOT INHERIT THE REVERSIBILITY OF THE THING HOSTED: the map is a bijection and the program calls STORE on every turn of the loop, and AB2 measured STORE at the full 9.5098 bits. A reversible mathematics implemented on an erasing machine still erases, which is the gap between having a property and running it.

predictions.claim: the ladder exceeds a tryte at term 15, so never forgetting is unaffordable in bounded memory
predictions.note: The ladder grows like phi^n and a tryte holds -364..+364, so term 15 at 377 does not fit and fourteen do. Asked for eighteen terms the machine emits 233 then -352, wrapping rather than growing, which is the only thing bounded memory can do. THE PRICE OF A TRAJECTORY GRAPH THAT CANNOT CONVERGE IS A STATE THAT CANNOT BE BOUNDED. Every real machine erases for exactly this reason, and an implied receipt has to buy its way out of that trade rather than assume it away -- which is what AJ1 shows is possible, since reversibility gets the non-convergence without the unbounded state.
predictions.at_risk: NOT AT RISK: "exceeds a tryte at term 15, where 377 > 364": the comparison is performed in the registration. CONTESTABLE: the audit flagged this one as among the six of its 25 it would concede; see `reaudits` for how a verdict is moved.

prediction_sets.subject: The smallest reversible ternary language, and the trilemma it exposes

predictions.claim: the three primitive forms are a universal reversible language: every instance a permutation of order 3, generating A_27
predictions.note: All fifteen gate instances are permutations of the 27 states and every one has order exactly 3, so a program's inverse is that program with each gate applied twice more and THE LANGUAGE NEEDS NO INVERSE INSTRUCTION SET. The group they generate is A_27, agreeing with M's recorded figure from an implementation written separately -- two independent codings landing on one 28-digit number is what makes a re-implementation worth having. ERRATUM, AND THE REASON IT IS ONLY AN ERRATUM: the registration typed A_27 as a 25-digit number, dropping three zeros, so the decimal expansion in the prediction was wrong by a factor of a thousand. The tool COMPUTES 27!/2 rather than comparing against the typed digits, which is why a transcription slip in the registration is a footnote instead of a false verdict. AGENTS.md already says to derive constants and never hardcode them; the tool obeyed it and the prose did not.
predictions.argument: Each form adds a fixed amount mod 3 to one trit under a condition on another, so three applications return every state. Order exactly 3 by construction, which is what makes the inverse derivable and an inverse instruction set unnecessary.

predictions.claim: reversibility is inherited by composition, so every program has in-degree 1 with no analysis
predictions.note: Four hundred random programs of random length, and every one has in-degree exactly 1 at all 27 states with zero unreachable. A composition of bijections is a bijection, so THERE IS NOTHING A PROGRAMMER CAN WRITE IN THIS LANGUAGE THAT BREAKS IT. Compare what factor four cost everywhere else: AI4 had to search 19,683 tables to find the 216 that work, and AJ1 needed the map to be built out of addition on purpose. Here it costs no analysis, no search and no discipline -- it is a property of the alphabet rather than of the program.
predictions.at_risk: NOT AT RISK: A composition of bijections is a bijection, and the registration says so. The manifest's own argument field concedes it: "the 400 sampled were a check on the implementation, never the grounds for the claim".
predictions.argument: A composition of bijections is a bijection. Every primitive is a bijection, so in-degree 1 holds for every program that can be written — the 400 sampled were a check on the implementation, never the grounds for the claim.

predictions.claim: a straight-line reversible program costs its own length for every input, so the cost spread is exactly 1.00 and factor three is lost
predictions.note: Every one of fifty straight-line programs costs exactly its own length in gates, for all 27 starting states: a spread of 1.0000. That is FLATTER THAN THE 1.02x AG1 CALLED SECURITY THEATRE, and against the 513.8x AH1 needed. Nothing in the language depends on the data, because branching on data means testing data and a test that discards its answer is erasing. So going fully reversible BUYS FACTOR FOUR AND LOSES FACTOR THREE, and the alternative registered -- that some program would show a spread above 1.00 and the worry was unfounded -- did not occur on any of them.
predictions.at_risk: NOT AT RISK: Cost is defined as gate count and the language has no branching, so a straight-line program's spread of exactly 1.00 restates the cost model.

predictions.claim: a trilemma: in-degree one, a cost that varies, and bounded state are available two at a time and never three

measured.hailstone_and_three_word: cost varies + bounded state, in-degree above 1
measured.history_growth: at least one trit per data-dependent step

predictions.note: Six constructions from this corpus tabulated against the three properties, and NONE HAS ALL THREE. The reversible language has in-degree one and bounded state with a flat cost; hailstone and the three-word program have a varying cost and bounded state with trajectories that merge; and buying the first two together is Bennett's construction -- a reversible machine CAN branch on data, but only by keeping the record of which way it went, so the history grows at least one trit per branch. A thousand data-dependent steps costs 167 trytes that can never be discarded, and AJ4 already measured what happens when bounded memory meets a state that will not stop growing: it wraps at term fifteen. IN-DEGREE ONE, A COST THAT VARIES, BOUNDED STATE -- PICK TWO.

prediction_sets.subject: The two-input ternary operations as a labelled task ladder for a grokking experiment

predictions.claim: exactly 27 of the 19,683 two-input ternary operations are affine over GF(3), and 18 of the 216 reversible ones are
predictions.note: Exact. 27 = 3^3, one per (alpha, beta, gamma). The reversible count of 216 reproduces AB1 from a criterion written independently, and the 18 affine-reversible is 2 x 3 x 3 because alpha must be nonzero for every column to be a bijection -- AB1 measured that same 18 by checking affineness of tables it had already found reversible, so the two routes cross-check rather than restate. THE POINT IS THE FRACTION: the grokking literature studies a task drawn from 0.137% of this space and holds the algebraic variable fixed while sweeping everything else.
predictions.at_risk: NOT AT RISK: 27 = 3^3 affine tables by parameter counting, and the 18 affine-and-reversible was already AB1's measured number. The manifest's own argument field concedes it: "Parameter counting, exhaustive by construction."
predictions.argument: 27 = 3^3, one affine table per (alpha, beta, gamma). The 18 affine-and-reversible is 2 x 3 x 3 because alpha must be nonzero for every column to be a bijection. Parameter counting, exhaustive by construction.

predictions.claim: affine is exactly the set a linear map can fit, and nothing else reaches a perfect fit
predictions.note: Exhaustive over every (alpha,beta,gamma) and every table. Exactly 27 reach 9 of 9 rows and they are exactly the affine ones; the best any non-affine table manages is 8 of 9, and 486 of them get that close. So the label is not a convention -- it is precisely what a model with no nonlinearity can represent, and 19,656 tables need one. Modular addition, the literature task, is among the 27.
predictions.at_risk: NOT AT RISK: A perfect linear fit over every row IS the definition of affine, so "fails on all 19,656 others" restates the definition. CONTESTABLE: the audit flagged this one as among the six of its 25 it would concede; see `reaudits` for how a verdict is moved.

predictions.claim: all four quadrants are non-empty and the erasure varies within each
predictions.note: The quadrant counts held exactly -- 18, 9, 198, 19,458, totalling 19,683 -- and the independence claim with them: reversibility and affineness really are separate axes. The variation clause FAILED, and for a reason that is itself a result. Both REVERSIBLE quadrants are pinned at exactly 1.585 bits with no spread at all, because reversible-in-the-leading-argument means every column is a bijection, so each output value appears exactly three times across the nine pairs and the erasure is log2(3) by construction. Only the erasing quadrants vary. Note also that this column measures the OUTPUT map, nine pairs onto three values, and not AB2 pair map which preserves the second argument -- the same distinction AJ2 drew, arriving again unbidden.

predictions.claim: the arena ladder is 9, 729 and 531,441 examples, and the three-trit arena is within an order of magnitude of mod-113 addition
predictions.note: The counts held; the comparison failed. 729 against 12,769 is a factor of 17.5, which is not within an order of magnitude however generously read -- the canonical setup sits BETWEEN the three-trit arena and the six-trit one rather than beside either. The ladder still brackets it, which is what an experiment needs, but the sentence claimed something tidier than the arithmetic supports and the arithmetic was available before the claim was written.

prediction_sets.subject: Does the algebra of a task predict when a network generalises? A grokking sweep with the algebraic label as the variable

predictions.claim: grokking reproduces on this task family at all, with a gap of at least 5x between memorisation and generalisation
predictions.note: Held with room to spare. Both reversible tasks memorise 292 training pairs by step 200 and do not reach 90% on the 437 held-out pairs until thousands of steps later -- gaps of 36x and 19x against a predicted 5x. So the phenomenon reproduces on a family that is NOT modular arithmetic, and whose hidden structure is a base-three FACTORISATION rather than a Fourier basis: the network sees a and b as opaque tokens in 0..26 and has to discover that the operation is positionwise in base three.

predictions.claim: the affine task groks soonest, so the algebraic label predicts the outcome
predictions.note: FAILED, and it inverted rather than merely missing. The AFFINE task -- ternary modular addition, which is what the grokking literature studies almost exclusively -- is the SLOWER of the two on every paired seed, with a median of 10,800 steps against 6,200, and on one seed it never reached 90% at all inside a 40,000-step budget while the non-affine task generalised on all five. Run once this would be a draw; run five times with everything but the algebra held fixed it is a direction. THE CANONICAL GROKKING TASK IS HARDER THAN A NON-AFFINE SIBLING, which is a comparison the literature has not been able to make because it has no labelled task ladder to make it on. Stated limit: one table per quadrant, so this measures seed-stability and not table-stability, and sweeping tables within a quadrant is the obvious next thing.

predictions.claim: the erasing tasks have a majority-class baseline above 40% while the reversible ones sit near 3.7%
predictions.note: FAILED, and the reasoning behind it was the error. I conflated "erases in the leading argument" with "has a skewed output distribution", and they are different properties. The affine-erasing table is f = b, which is a BIJECTION in its second argument, so its outputs are perfectly uniform and its baseline is 0.0457 -- identical to the reversible tasks. Only tritwise MIN is genuinely skewed, at 0.1918, and even that is far short of 40%. AL3 had already shown the erasure column for that quadrant spans 1.585 to 3.170 and the table chosen sat at the uniform end, so the information needed to avoid this was on the record before the prediction was written.

predictions.claim: the affine-erasing quadrant is degenerate and is learned within a tenth of the steps the affine-reversible task needs
predictions.note: Held at 0.028 against a predicted tenth: 200 steps versus 7,200, with no memorisation-to-generalisation gap at all. And it is degenerate BY PROOF rather than by luck -- an affine table is reversible in its leading argument exactly when alpha is nonzero, so affine AND erasing forces alpha = 0 and the function ignores its first input entirely. All nine tables in that quadrant are one-input functions, so the prediction covers the quadrant and not just the table trained.

prediction_sets.subject: Does a purpose-built search puzzle have the find-against-verify asymmetry? A ternary proof-of-work candidate, exhaustive over all 531,441 message-nonce pairs

predictions.claim: the variance of hit counts across messages separates a compressing puzzle from a relabelling, landing within 25% of binomial at every difficulty while a bijective candidate gives exactly zero
predictions.note: FAILED at two of six difficulties, and the failure is the whole result. Two of the three legs held: the mean first hit sat within 15% of the finite-population null at every k, and both bijective controls gave a hit-count variance of EXACTLY zero against a binomial 12.73 -- which is the discriminator D4 could not supply, since truncating any permutation gives perfectly uniform buckets and a collision count therefore cannot separate a hash from a relabelling. The leg that failed is the one that mattered. The candidate came in at 0.729x and 0.674x of binomial at k = 1 and k = 2, MORE uniform than chance, and a puzzle more uniform than chance is structured. Chasing that deviation found the structure (see F-MESSAGE-COMMUTES-OUT-OF-A-GROUP-FEEDFORWARD). The registration said in advance that agreement would not be a certificate and that only disagreement could refute; the disagreement arrived and did exactly that.

predictions.claim: the tabulator kills a bijective puzzle and the algebra kills an affine one, both at one operation per solve, with affine strictly worse because it needs no table
predictions.note: Held on every clause. AD2 tabulated a program to price it and broke even at seventy queries; here the same attack breaks a bijective puzzle outright at one lookup, because a permutation can be walked backwards from the target. The affine candidate is strictly worse: the nonce is a rotation of a difference, so there is nothing to precompute but a single 6x6 inversion and the attack is profitable on query one. The gap between the two is exactly the 729-entry table. So the two algebraic labels this project has carried since AL are, for a puzzle, both disqualifying -- and in a strict order.

predictions.claim: a puzzle that is non-invertible in the nonce strands messages at the null rate, and a bijective one strands none
predictions.note: Held, and it is the symmetric twin of the receipt result. The receipt died needing in-degree one; the puzzle NEEDS in-degree above one, or AN2(a) inverts it -- and pays for that in messages no nonce can mine. At maximum difficulty 264 of 729 messages, 36.2%, have no solution at all, and a miner holding one grinds forever. Both bijective controls strand exactly zero, so the property that guarantees every message is mineable is the same property that lets an attacker skip the mining. The number survives the keyed reconstruction (35 and 283), which is what shows the result is about compression rather than about this particular construction.

predictions.claim: widening the nonce cures the stranding and the understated work at once, because both are one symptom of the nonce space failing to outrun the target rarity
predictions.note: Held on both halves, and they moved together. A twelve-trit nonce absorbed in two blocks through the same compression function strands nothing at maximum difficulty and raises the mean search from 311.2 to 735.0, which is within 0.8% of 3^6 = 729 -- the figure a proper lottery owes and the one a truncated nonce space understates by 58%. So AN3 is not a fact about irreversibility as such but about a nonce space too small for the target, and the design rule is measured rather than borrowed: nonce space must exceed target rarity by orders of magnitude. That is what the extraNonce field in Bitcoin is for.

prediction_sets.subject: Can an erasing machine certify that a secret was wiped? Ceremony maps over 729 secrets, and whether the erasure measure is the right certificate

predictions.claim: the pseudorandom ceremony map measures E within 5% of the 0.8265 null while exposing, within 10% of 268, secrets whose preimage is a single point

measured.control_draw_position: 2.09 sd from the mean of 400 draws

predictions.note: FAILED on the erasure clause and held on the one that carried the argument, and the post-mortem is worth more than either. E came in at 0.8894 against a null of 0.8265 -- 7.6% out where 5% was registered. Sweeping 400 pseudorandom maps then showed the null was exactly right (mean 0.8269, sd 0.0299) and that 336 of 400 draws WOULD have passed the 5% band. The band was reasonable; the draw was not. This set fixed one seed as its control and happened to fix a 2.09-sigma one, so the failure is about the sample and not about the criterion or the claim. A SINGLE FIXED PSEUDORANDOM MAP CANNOT BE SCORED AGAINST A DISTRIBUTIONAL NULL: it is one sample and the null is a spread. The exposed clause survived on the same unlucky draw only because it was given a 10% band rather than a 5% one. And the substance held completely: 252 of 729 secrets, 34.6%, are recovered EXACTLY from the public output while the average erasure reads healthy at 0.89 bits. E is a mean and hiding is a minimum.

predictions.claim: truncating the mixer to m trits gives every output exactly 3^(6-m) preimages, minimum equal to maximum, while the pseudorandom map has a minimum of 1
predictions.argument: The mixer is a bijection, so the 729 secrets land on 729 distinct values; grouping those by their low m trits partitions them into 3^m classes of exactly 3^(6-m). Flatness is forced by the pigeonhole equality, not observed -- and it holds at every width where the truncation divides the space.
predictions.note: Held exactly at every m from 1 to 5. The point is the reuse: D4 FAILED because truncating any permutation gives perfectly uniform buckets, which made a collision count useless as evidence of mixing. That same forced uniformity is precisely what a wipe wants -- every secret hidden among exactly as many others as every other secret, with no output easier to invert than another. A construction disqualified as a hash test is the right answer to a different question, and the disqualifying property IS the qualifying one.

predictions.claim: truncation attains the pigeonhole hiding bound at every power of three and the pseudorandom map attains it nowhere
predictions.note: Held on both clauses. The bound itself is arithmetic -- every preimage of at least h forces an image of at most floor(729/h) -- so what was at risk was attainment, and the split is total: truncation attains it at all four, the pseudorandom map at none, and not one of 400 random draws is even flat. A balanced wipe does not happen by accident. The exchange rate is the useful number: to hide every secret among 27 others the public output may carry 4.755 of its 9.510 bits, so HIDING IS BOUGHT WITH OUTPUT BITS at a fixed price, and a ceremony whose parameters must be large enough to be useful cannot buy much of it.

predictions.claim: the count of fully-exposed secrets lands within 10% of both the 268 null and AN3's measured 264 stranded blocks, because both are tails of the same Poisson(1)

measured.reason: P(Poisson(1)=0) = P(Poisson(1)=1) = 1/e, so the two tails are equal by construction

predictions.note: Held on both comparisons. A block with no winning nonce and a secret with a unique preimage are the k=0 and k=1 tails of the same Poisson(1), and Poisson(1) puts identical mass on those two, so the counts are equal by construction rather than by coincidence. AN3 measured 264 unmineable blocks; AO measures 252 unhidden secrets; the shared null is 268. Two results this project reached by different routes, four sets apart, are the same number, and neither set knew it.

prediction_sets.subject: Can a hash-only key layer give a minted coin an owner? Lamport one-time signatures at base two and base three, exhaustive over 729 messages

predictions.claim: an attacker holding one valid signature can forge exactly one message, the one already signed
predictions.note: Held exhaustively. Every one of the 729 signed messages forges exactly itself and nothing else, so the scheme is not broken at first use -- which is the assumption everything else in the set rests on. The controls pin both ends of the meter: holding no signature forges nothing, holding all of them forges everything.

predictions.claim: two signatures under one key leak at the binomial rate, mean within 5% of 21.43, maximum 64 and minimum 1

measured.maximum_is: 2^6, when the messages differ in all six positions
measured.minimum_is: signing the same message twice, which reveals nothing new

predictions.note: Held on all three clauses, and the mean agrees with the closed form to one part in ten thousand -- which is the real content, because it confirms the binomial model is the right description of what a reused key gives away rather than merely a plausible one. The one-time restriction is therefore not advisory: a second signature under the same key hands away 2.94% of the message space on average and 8.78% at worst, and there is no configuration in which it hands away nothing unless the same message is signed twice.

predictions.claim: ternary leaks less of its own space than binary on key reuse, 2.94% against 5.63%
predictions.at_risk: NOT AT RISK: The project's own verdict at the time, already recorded in the note and in should_not_have_been_registered: both sides are the closed form (1 + (b-1)/b)^pos and the registration computed both before the run.

measured.mechanism: trits differ with p = 2/3 against bits at 1/2, so the per-position rate is HIGHER for ternary and the leak is still lower, because the position count falls faster

predictions.note: Held, including the mechanism clause -- ternary digits collide more often and leak less anyway, because six positions against ten outweighs two thirds against one half. But it should not have been registered. Both sides are the closed form (1 + (b-1)/b)^pos and the registration itself computed both before the run, so nothing here was ever at risk. AGENTS.md names this failure directly: inflating the registered set with facts that were never at risk turns the discipline into decoration. Recorded as held and as a registration that should not have been made.

predictions.claim: ternary pays for that advantage in destruction: 12 of 18 preimages against 10 of 20, and strictly more erased bits
predictions.at_risk: NOT AT RISK: The project's own verdict at the time, already recorded in the note and in should_not_have_been_registered: (b-1)/b and the projection erasure are closed forms over a scheme whose base and position count the registration stipulated.
predictions.note: Held. The wipe is a projection from a b-tuple of preimages onto the one revealed, and AB's own erasure measure agrees with the closed form log2(ALPHA^(b-1)) exactly, so the ternary key destroys 19.020 bits of material against binary's 15.850. AP3's leak advantage is bought with a larger wipe, and AO already priced what a wipe costs. Like AP3 this was arithmetic before it was measured: (b-1)/b and the projection erasure are both closed forms, and the only thing genuinely measured was that erasureOf agrees with them.

prediction_sets.subject: How wide should an authenticated tree be, and does a power of three ever beat a power of two? A cost model over every integer branching factor from 2 to 1024, 45 leaf counts, and a bytes-per-verify-operation exchange rate swept across eight decades

predictions.claim: binary is never optimal for a vector commitment, the optimum never descends past three, and across the swept leaf counts THREE is the large-gamma optimum more often than four
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: the first half leans on a continuous argument and this set exists because ceilings break those. depth(N, 2) can fall well below the smooth law at particular N, and one cell with argmin 2 refutes it. The second half -- which of 3 and 4 wins more leaf counts -- I cannot call at all.
predictions.note: Failed on its last clause, and that clause was the whole point. The first three parts held exactly: no cell in 2,880 has argmin 2, the optimum never goes below 3, and it never widens as verifying gets dearer. But three does not beat four at the verify-dominated limit -- it TIES, 21 leaf counts each. Chasing the tie produced F-TREE-BRANCHES-IN-ITS-OWN-BASE, which is a better answer than the one predicted: 3^k leaf counts want three and 2^k leaf counts want four, so the tie was a property of how many of each shape this sweep contains rather than of trees. T-CLAIM-NARROWED-BY-A-DESIGN, fourth bite. NARROWED AFTERWARDS, AND STATED HERE SO A READER OF AQ ALONE IS NOT MISLED: AR4 lifted the constant-arity constraint every tree in this sweep was built under, and F-TREE-BRANCHES-IN-ITS-OWN-BASE turned out to be a property of CONSTANT trees rather than of trees. 25 of these 45 leaf counts change shape once radix sequences are admitted, 11 of the 18 powers of three among them, and N = 729 wants [4,4,4,4,3] rather than six threes -- for 0.0178% of the total cost, a surface flat to four decimal places. AR's evidence for that is FREQUENCY and not magnitude: its null over 100 redraws has a tail reaching 23.7%, ABOVE the subject's own worst cell, so a structureless per-level cost can produce a larger maximum than the real regime does, while the frequency of improvement separates a hundredfold. T-CLAIM-NARROWED-BY-A-DESIGN, fifth bite, and the second time the class has bitten this same sentence.

predictions.claim: counting cells whose cost-minimising branching factor is a power of three against those where it is a power of two, three takes strictly more, despite ten powers of two being in range against six of three
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: entirely, and the arithmetic starts against it. Ten powers of two sit in 2..1024 and only six powers of three, so the geometry has to overcome a handicap of almost two to one.
predictions.note: The handicap was real and the geometry did not overcome it: two takes 1,044 cells to three's 821. But PER ARITY IN RANGE the ordering reverses -- each power of three wins 137 cells against each power of two's 104 -- so the registered wording measured how many of each arity I put in the sweep as much as it measured the trees. The claim was answerable only because a design decision had already half-decided it.

predictions.claim: unit invariance FAILS: recomputing every cost in whole trytes rather than whole bytes moves at least one argmin, because a proof travels in whole units and that rounding is a ceiling a bare scale factor is not

The escape is that a proof travels in whole units, so rounding each term up reintroduces a ceiling, and near-ties between adjacent arities are common enough that one should flip. If this fails, the unit is free and that is worth knowing too.
predictions.note: Held, registered deliberately against the obvious answer that a scale factor cannot move an argmin. Eight cells of 2,880 flip, all of them near-ties between adjacent arities, exactly as the argument said they would. It held for the right reason on an effect thirteen times smaller than the instrument first reported: the registered conversion divided a COUNT OF OPERATIONS by bytes-per-tryte and rounded it, a category error twice over, and showed 103. Caught before scoring because a 19% unit change cannot honestly move an optimum from three to six. T-INSTRUMENT-FALSE-VERDICT, eighteenth bite. The wrong conversion is kept in the tool and both numbers are pinned, so the fix cannot silently regress.

predictions.claim: at every cell where either arity is within 15% of that cell's optimum, the totals at branching factor 64 and 256 differ by no more than 15%
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: this is the question that was actually asked, and 15% is a number picked before looking -- wide enough to be interesting, narrow enough to fail. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ node tools/branching-audit.js
predictions.note: Failed and not narrowly -- 571 of 909, worst case 149%. But 426 of those 571 are cells where 64 and 256 sit at DIFFERENT DEPTHS, and when 256 saves a whole level it wins by that level while when it does not it pays four times the verify for nothing. So the two are close to interchangeable at a fixed depth and completely different across a depth step, which makes the answer a fact about the leaf count rather than about either arity. prediction_sets.subject: What happens when a tree's arity is allowed to VARY by depth? AQ's cost model extended from radices to radix sequences, over AQ's 45 leaf counts at all 64 exchange rates and over EVERY integer leaf count from 2 to 8,192 at the eight decade rates

predictions.claim: letting the arity vary is worth less than a sixth: at every cell of both vector-regime sweeps the best radix sequence costs at least 85% of the best constant arity's cost
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: this comes out the other way if ONE leaf count anywhere in [2, 8192] has a factorisation that leaves the constant optimiser worse stranded than N = 11 did. Five leaf counts worked on paper give 1.5%, 4.0%, 4.2%, 7.1% and 9.99%, the last found by deliberately hunting a bad case, so the line stands about 50% above the worst thing five attempts could find and is refuted by a single cell past it. Five of 8,236 leaf counts is not a sample I can extrapolate from; the corners those five did not visit are the bytes-dominated rates and the very small counts.
predictions.note: Held, and the bound is worth less than it looks. The worst cell in 68,408 is 12.30% at N = 257 and the worst on AQ's own grid is 9.99% at N = 128, both inside the registered 15%. But the post-hoc null over 100 redraws has a TAIL reaching 23.7%, above the subject's worst cell, so a structureless per-level cost can produce a larger maximum than the real regime does and magnitude discriminates nothing here. What discriminates is frequency, which is AR3. The line's placement decided this verdict: a 10% line would have FAILED at 12.30%, and the reason for widening it to 15% -- a hand case at 9.99% that would have made 10% a coin toss -- was on the record before the run. predictions.claim: the staircase flattens by more than half: over the deep contiguous window at the verify-dominated rate, the largest single-leaf relative cost jump is less than half as large when arity may vary as when it may not
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: this comes out the other way if the varying tree has a single bad step anywhere the constant tree happens to be smooth, because both sides are MAXIMA over 7,167 consecutive pairs and they need not occur at the same leaf count. I have one pair on paper, N = 1,024 -> 1,025, where the constant jump is 11.97% and the varying jump 4.00%; where either maximum actually sits is not something arithmetic hands me, and if the varying maximum sits somewhere other than 1,025 the ratio can be anything.

The unregistered robustness windows show the statistic is not universal: over [8192, 16384] the CONSTANT cost is perfectly flat, because 4^7 = 16384 covers the whole octave, so the constant tree pays a fixed premium for a full-size tree while the varying tree tracks the leaf count and is therefore both cheaper and raggeder. Tightness against the ceiling is bought with raggedness.

predictions.claim: variation helps most leaf counts, not a few: over the deep contiguous window at the verify-dominated rate, more than half of the leaf counts have a strictly cheaper varying optimum
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: AT RISK, AND THIS IS THE ONE I CANNOT CALL: it comes out the other way if the constant optimiser's freedom to pick its own depth is worth as much as the sequence's freedom to pick its own widths, and I have no way to settle that short of running it. The reasoning FOR is that a constant tree must round every level up together while a sequence rounds only a minority of them, so equality needs the rounding remainder to land on 0 or on d, roughly a 2/(d+1) coincidence. The evidence AGAINST is my own: of six leaf counts I worked by hand, four were NOT helped. I am registering the reasoning against my own sample, which is the choice that can embarrass me, and if the sample is right rather than the reasoning then the flexibility is a rarity rather than a rule and `AR1`'s bound describes a corner case.

I registered the reasoning against my own hand sample and the reasoning was right; the sample was drawn at powers, which is where a constant tree is at its best. The unhelped 1,025 are EXACTLY the leaf counts whose optimal tree is a constant arity, with no exceptions in 7,169 -- and those are powers of FOUR rather than powers in general, since four is the arity the optimum wants. 2187 = 3^7 is helped.

predictions.claim: the optimal tree gets deeper more often than shallower: over the deep contiguous window at the verify-dominated rate, leaf counts whose varying optimum is strictly deeper than their constant optimum outnumber those whose varying optimum is strictly shallower
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: it comes out the other way if the per-level bytes charge O outweighs the per-level rounding slack, and I have a worked case where it does -- at N = 10^8 the hand arithmetic puts the varying optimum THREE levels SHALLOWER than the constant one, which is the direction opposite to the one registered. Both declared tie-breaks also push against it: the constant baseline breaks ties toward the smaller arity and so toward the deeper tree, and the sequence breaks ties toward the smaller depth and so toward the shallower one. The reasoning FOR is only that the slack a sequence exploits is per-level, so there is more of it where there are more levels.
predictions.note: FAILED, and inverted rather than narrowly missed: 3,580 shallower against 2,176 deeper, 1.6 to 1. The registered reasoning had the mechanism backwards. It argued that more levels means more per-level slack to exploit, so the tree should grow. What a sequence actually buys is the SAME verify budget in FEWER levels: the quantity gamma is charged on is never larger than the constant tree's, it is identical at 2,861 of 7,169 leaf counts, and 1,836 of the 3,580 shallower cells are of exactly that kind. THE SLACK REMOVES A LEVEL RATHER THAN ADDING ONE, and the saving there is level overhead rather than work. That mechanism is what overturns AQ's headline: 25 of AQ's 45 leaf counts change shape, 11 of the 18 powers of three among them, and N = 729 wants [4,4,4,4,3] rather than six threes -- for 0.0178% of the total cost.

prediction_sets.subject: Does the mixer's residual algebra help a ledger forger? Four designed attacks on D's split-round chain as a ledger head -- a cross-ledger census of the compensating family over 2,000 drawn ledgers, the differential table of g = P - I, a delta ordering built from it, and a meet-in-the-middle join over four modified entries -- each priced in a cost model stated before the run

predictions.claim: the 26 is a fact about the mixer and not about one ledger, and there is no weak ledger class: over 2,000 independently drawn six-entry ledgers swept over all 10,920 distinct compensating forgeries each, the mean accept count lands within 0.6 of the chance value 14.979, the variance-to-mean ratio lands in [0.80, 1.25], and no single ledger accepts more than 40
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: it comes out the other way if the chain's non-flatness reaches the forgery neighbourhood. `F-MIXER-HEAD-IS-NOT-FLAT` measured this same chain running 629 to 851 preimages against a flat 729 at length two — a spread of about 17% — and if a six-entry ledger's accept rate inherits a spread of that size then the per-ledger rate is 1/729 times (1 + e) with e of order 0.17, the variance-to-mean ratio is 1 + 15 x 0.17^2 = 1.43 rather than 1, and the line at 1.25 fails. The evidence I have pointing the other way is one ledger: 13 distinct accepts against 14.979, which is 0.5 sd low and tells me nothing about dispersion, since a single draw has no dispersion. The line at 40 is placed where noise cannot reach it — Poisson(14.979) puts under one ledger in four million there — so it can only fire on a real class of weak ledgers.
predictions.note: Held on all three legs. The mean is 1.5 standard errors above chance, the dispersion is Poisson to within 2%, and the worst of 2,000 ledgers accepts 30 against a line at 40. The 17% preimage spread F-MIXER-HEAD-IS-NOT-FLAT measured at length two does NOT reach the six-entry forgery neighbourhood: had it, the registered arithmetic put the ratio at 1.43 and the line at 1.25 would have fired. Two further structural cuts were looked at and neither is a lever -- no merge distance and no carry pattern accepts above 1.05x chance, so the arithmetic-versus-tritwise group mismatch that a forger might have exploited buys nothing at this width. What this does NOT say is that the 26 was a good number to publish: the published sweep counts every forgery twice, so 26 of 21,840 is 13 of 10,920 (F-COMPENSATING-SWEEP-DOUBLE-COUNTS), and 13 against 14.979 is 0.5 sd low rather than the 13% deficit the ordered pair suggests.

predictions.claim: there is no strong differential in the residual algebra: the differential table of g over GF(3)^6, over all 728 non-zero input differences and all 729 output differences, has a maximum cell of at most 27, so no input-to-output difference through g holds with probability better than 1/27
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: the split round is a Feistel over Z27 x Z27 — (lo, hi) becomes (hi, lo + S[hi]) mod 27 — and in THAT group it has a two-round characteristic that holds with probability one, since an input difference confined to `lo` leaves `hi` untouched, so the S-box is never active and the difference merely swaps halves. Eight rounds contain four such windows. If that characteristic survives into the tritwise metric this table maxes out in the hundreds and the prediction fails by an order of magnitude. What I have pointing the other way is that the round's addition is mod 27 while the difference here is measured digit-wise mod 3, so a fixed tritwise difference does not even correspond to a fixed mod-27 difference, and a random function's maximum over 530,712 cells is only about 10. I cannot settle which effect wins without running it; the line at 27 is placed at one active S-box's worth of probability, well above the random maximum and well below what one surviving free round would produce, so neither outcome is noise.
predictions.note: Held, and by a wider margin than the registration expected: the maximum is 8, not merely under 27. The Feistel's free two-round characteristic -- probability one in the mod-27 group, four windows in eight rounds -- does not survive into the tritwise metric at all, which is the mechanism the registration named as the way this could fail by an order of magnitude. The number that makes the verdict readable is the control: over twelve random permutations the same statistic runs 7 to 9 and the empty-cell fraction 36.81% against g's 36.74%, so g's differential behaviour is not distinguishable from a random permutation's residual. ONE DISCLOSURE. The registration's own null arithmetic put a random function's maximum at 9 to 11; the measured controls say 7 to 9. The null was slightly wrong, it was arithmetic rather than measurement, and it decided nothing, because the line was at 27 and the answer was 8. The affine control returning exactly 729 is what says the statistic could have reached the hundreds.

predictions.claim: the meet-in-the-middle join does not beat its own ideal yield: the four-position join returns between 0.97 and 1.10 times the ideal 531,441 forgeries, on the canonical ledger and on every one of eight independently drawn ones
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: both halves of the join are images of the same `g` — the left is a four-step push forward and the right a two-step pull backward — and the key counts average exactly one per key, so this is a join of two sparse tables. If their reachable key sets coincide rather than being independent, the join returns the sum of squared counts rather than the product of means, which for counts distributed Poisson(1) is 2.0 times ideal, not 1.0. That is a factor of two in a forger's yield sitting on whether two derived distributions are correlated, and I have nothing on paper that settles it: the argument for independence is that the left key's second coordinate is an arithmetic partial sum which is exactly flat and carries no `g` structure at all, and the argument against is that both accumulator coordinates are sums of `g`-values over the same 729-point image. A ratio below 0.97 refutes it in the other direction and would mean the two halves ANTI-correlate, which would be a stronger structural finding than the prediction.
predictions.note: Held, and it was the one the registration said could not be called. The two half-tables are genuinely sparse -- 335,881 and 335,763 of 531,441 keys occupied, meeting on 212,371 -- so the failure mode was live: had their reachable key sets coincided the join would have returned the sum of squared counts, which the tool measures at 2.0003 for this very table. It returns 1.0020 instead. The non-flatness F-MIXER-HEAD-IS-NOT-FLAT found is real and is NOT cashable here, and a chain built on a random permutation gives 1.0000, so the mixer's structure buys the forger nothing in yield. The value of the result is what it licenses: the join is a complete enumeration of the four-position family at 6.99 ops per forgery, and that is the cost figure the ledger question actually turns on.

predictions.claim: ordering deltas by the differential table more than halves the forger's trials: over the same 2,000 ledgers, restricted to the five adjacent position pairs and to cases where at least one of the 728 deltas is accepted, the mean rank of the first accepted delta under a differential-table-descending order with ties broken uniformly is less than 0.5 times the mean rank under a uniformly random order
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: the exclusion of empty cells alone caps the gain at 0.63, because about 36.8% of cells are empty for a random function and a delta whose cell is empty cannot be accepted at all. Everything below 0.63 has to come from the table's TAIL being heavy enough that the top-ranked cells carry a share of the accepts far above their share of the deltas — for Poisson(1) cells the 8% of cells holding 3 or more carry 26.4% of the mass, which lands the ratio near 0.30 and holds. If instead `g`'s table is FLATTER than a random function's, the ordering degenerates to the empty-cell filter and the ratio lands at 0.63 and this fails. That is not hypothetical: `AN1` registered this same mixer's hit variance as binomial and it came in LOW at two difficulties — more uniform than chance — which is the exact direction that refutes this. I am registering against that observation.
predictions.note: Held at 0.4506 against a line at 0.5, and the margin needed a spread beside it rather than a point: the bootstrap 95% interval is [0.4425, 0.4589] and two further seeds give 0.4495 and 0.4566, none of them reaching the line. AN1's finding -- that this mixer's hit variance came in LOW, more uniform than chance -- was the registered route to failure and it did not transfer: g's differential table is as heavy-tailed as a random function's, with 8.01% of cells holding three or more and those cells carrying 26.4% of the mass, against the 26.4% the Poisson null predicts. THE MECHANISM IS EXACT AND IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THE SET. An accepted forgery at an adjacent pair IS the realisation of a two-round differential, so a delta whose cell is empty cannot be accepted -- 0 accepts in 2,669,929 tries -- and the accept rate rises linearly with the cell, 0.98x chance at cell one to 6.65x at cell seven. A forger with the 531,441-entry table discards 36.67% of the family with certainty and finds the top 8.04% carrying 26.86% of the accepts.

prediction_sets.subject: What does an INSERTION cost a ledger forger? Set AS left the route open by naming it: P has one fixed point, so from every accumulator exactly one entry value leaves the mixer head unchanged, and every forgery in AS keeps the ledger at six entries. This set prices a forger who may lengthen it -- insert, delete and rearrange against a ledger publishing BOTH heads -- in two currencies stated before the run, operations and GROWTH, with no exchange rate invented between them

predictions.claim: insertion is paid for in LENGTH and the length is single digits: over 2,000 independently drawn six-entry ledgers, the minimum number of forced no-op insertions that restores BOTH heads, computed exactly by breadth-first search over Z_729 on that ledger's seven forced generators, has a mean in [4.0, 6.0] and no single ledger of the 2,000 needs more than 12
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: the counting heuristic that puts this at 4.87 -- 791 non-empty multisets of size at most five against 729 residues -- assumes the seven forced values behave like seven independent uniform draws, and they are seven reads of ONE map v(a) = val(u* - a) at seven accumulators of one chain. Two observations already on the record say that assumption is doubtful in the same direction. The accumulator after the first entry is a_0 + g(a_0 + e_1), and `AS` measured g's image at 465 of 729, so a_1 can take only 465 values rather than 729; and `F-MIXER-HEAD-IS-NOT-FLAT` measured this same chain at 629 to 851 preimages against a flat 729 at length two. If that shortfall compounds along the chain the seven generators are drawn from a shrinking support with repeats, the reachable sums are fewer than the heuristic assumes, and the mean climbs past 6.0 while the maximum climbs past 12. In the other direction, the gap-0 generator is the same on all 2,000 ledgers -- the accumulator before the first entry is the tritwise identity, so the prepend value is the constant val(u*) -- and if its order in Z_729 is 1 or 3, which is the three values 0 and plus or minus 243 of the 729 it could be, then a fixed run of at most three prepends forges every ledger, the minimum is bounded by three everywhere and the mean falls below 4.0. I have not computed val(u*): this repository records that `P` has one fixed point and nowhere records which one, and `AS` measured the no-op's EXISTENCE at all 729 accumulators and its value at none of them.
predictions.note: Held on both legs, at 4.934 against a registered band of [4.0, 6.0] and a worst ledger of 10 against a line at 12. Neither named failure route fired. The uniform-generator null measures 4.966 and a chain built on a random permutation 4.911, so THE SEVEN FORCED VALUES ARE NOT DISTINGUISHABLE FROM SEVEN INDEPENDENT UNIFORM DRAWS at this length -- g's image being 465 of 729 does not compound into a shrinking support the way the registration feared. The order census looks like structure and is not: 414.96 per 729 at order 729 against a null 486 is entirely the gap-0 generator counted once per ledger, since that one generator is the same constant on all 2,000 and has order 243. Remove it and the other 12,000 gaps give (4708 - 2000)/12000 = 0.2257 against a null 0.2222 and 7969/12000 = 0.664 against 0.6667. THE INTERESTING END IS THE LEFT ONE: 18 of the 2,000 ledgers have a minimum of 1, and those are exactly the chains that stand on the fixed point u* at some gap, where the forced no-op is arithmetically zero and a SINGLE inserted entry forges both heads. What this does not price is a forger who inserts values that are NOT no-ops; that forger needs two entries on every ledger and no search at all, which is F-A-UNIVERSAL-TWO-ENTRY-INSERTION-FORGERY and not this prediction.

predictions.claim: and that is not a property of length six: over ledger lengths 2 through 12 with 2,000 independently drawn ledgers at each length, the mean minimum insertion count is strictly decreasing at every one of the ten steps, lies above 9.0 at length two and below 4.5 at length twelve, and no single ledger at any length needs more than 100 insertions
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: the tightest predicted gap is the last one, 3.49 against 3.35, which at 2,000 ledgers a length is about five standard errors -- so noise cannot flip a step but structure can, and two routes would. If val(u*) has order at most 3 the gap-0 generator alone bounds the minimum at EVERY length, the curve is flat rather than decreasing and length two's mean falls under 9.0, so the monotone leg and the endpoint leg fail together. If instead long chains revisit accumulators more often than birthday chance -- thirteen gaps on 729 states collide with probability about 10% if the chain is flat, and `F-MIXER-HEAD-IS-NOT-FLAT` says it is not -- then a repeated accumulator contributes a DUPLICATE generator rather than a new one, the added gaps stop paying at the long end and a step breaks there. A maximum past 100 refutes the third leg and would mean some drawn ledger's forced values all lie in a proper subgroup of Z_729.
predictions.note: FAILED, on the third leg alone, and the failure is arithmetic I did myself rather than anything about the mixer. Three legs held: the mean is strictly decreasing at every one of the ten steps, 13.592 at length two is above 9.0, and 3.3625 at length twelve is below 4.5 -- and the whole curve tracks the uniform-generator null -- within 0.64 at length two and within 0.17 from length three on -- so a longer ledger really is cheaper to forge by insertion and it is cheaper for the counting reason and not a structural one. The fourth leg registered a bound on a MAXIMUM using a heuristic that is only about a MEAN. The exponential approximation that predicts 4.87 at length six -- accurate to 0.03 there -- puts the probability of a length-two ledger needing more than 100 insertions at essentially zero. Drawn directly, the uniform null exceeds 100 in 22, 25 and 33 of 50,000 draws at three seeds, so 2,000 draws expect about one and the line had roughly a 58% chance of firing on the null alone. The measured worst is 146; the null's own maximum over 50,000 draws is 243 at every seed. SO THE SUBJECT'S TAIL IS NOT HEAVIER THAN CHANCE and no claim is made that it is -- 146 against a single-draw null maximum of 81 is two samples from the same heavy tail. The lesson is the general one: a heuristic that is right about a mean can be wrong about a maximum by an order of magnitude, because the tail of this problem is governed by the cyclic subgroup a bad generator set generates rather than by counting multisets. T-CRITERION-IN-THE-NOISE, fourth bite.

predictions.claim: insertion has free parameters and deletion has none: over 2,000 drawn six-entry ledgers, (a) the two-free-insertion family -- 28 gap pairs p <= q, the first value free over all 729 and the second forced by the arithmetic total, so 20,412 candidates and a chance yield of 28.0 -- accepts with a mean within 2.0 of 28.0 and a variance-to-mean ratio in [0.80, 1.25]; and (b) at most 3 of the 2,000 ledgers admit any deletion-only forgery over all 63 non-empty subsets of their entries, against a chance expectation of 0.237 ledgers
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: half (a) can fail LOW and that is not a noise story. Fix a gap pair and let the free value run over all 729; the second value is then forced, so that pair's accept count is the number of preimages of one target under one map on 729 points. If that map is a PERMUTATION the count is exactly one for every pair on every ledger, the total is exactly 28 with variance ZERO, and the ratio fails at the bottom of its band rather than the top. The map is x -> STEP[push(STEP[a_p][x])][-x], whose first factor is a_p + g(a_p + x) and g is not injective -- its image is 465 of 729 -- so I expect random-function behaviour and a ratio near one. But `AN1` registered this same mixer's hit variance as binomial and it came in LOW at two difficulties, MORE UNIFORM THAN CHANCE, which is exactly the direction that drives this ratio to zero, and I am registering against that observation. Half (b) fails if the two conservation laws correlate on a deletion rather than being independent: for a single deletion the sum needs the entry to be arithmetically zero and the mixer needs the accumulator before it to be the fixed point, and if those coincide more often than one in 729 squared the count rises. Four or more ledgers is a one-in-ten-thousand event under Poisson(0.237), so that line can only fire on structure.
predictions.note: FAILED on half (a) by 0.012, and the miss is a real effect rather than a line flipped by noise: 30.0120 against 28.0 is seventeen standard errors, not a coin. The LINE was fine; the CHANCE VALUE was wrong, and the fact that makes it wrong was written into this set's own registration two hundred lines above the prediction. I4 says gap zero is the tritwise identity on every ledger. At a same-gap pair the map x -> STEP[STEP[a][x]][-x] is a composition of two bijections in the accumulator, so it is a PERMUTATION for every x, and the pair is accepted exactly when a is one of its fixed points; summed over all 729 accumulators that is 741, a mean of 1.0165, which is where 28 came from. But gap zero is not a draw from that distribution -- it is ONE NUMBER every ledger inherits, and for this chain it is 3. The family's true expectation is gapPairs - 1 + c(ZERO) = 30, and the measured 30.0120 sits 0.012 from it. The control settles it: a random-permutation chain has c(ZERO) = 0, its true expectation is 27, and it measures 27.1865. Half (b) held outright -- 0 of 2,000 ledgers admit a deletion-only forgery against a chance of 0.237, and the two conservation laws are visibly independent on that family: 173 of 126,000 subsets preserve the mixer head and 190 preserve the total, both at chance, and no subset does both. The registered failure route, a variance-to-mean ratio driven to zero by a permutation-like map, did not fire: 0.935. THE PRICE OF THE FAILURE IS THE FINDING -- c(ZERO) = 3 is F-A-UNIVERSAL-TWO-ENTRY-INSERTION-FORGERY, which is worth more than the prediction was.

predictions.claim: the two heads have complementary blind spots and reordering is the sum's: every rearrangement preserves the arithmetic total exactly, so the summed head accepts all of them; predicted that the mixer catches them at chance and no better -- over 2,000 drawn six-entry ledgers, sweeping all 720 permutations of each exhaustively, the total number of accepted distinct non-identity rearrangements is within 15% of the exact chance expectation of about 1,972, with a variance-to-mean ratio in [0.80, 1.25] and no single ledger accepting more than 10
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: `AS` proved this chain's head is a COMMUTATIVE SUM. D2 says head = g(u_1) + ... + g(u_L) in the reparametrised variable u_k = a_{k-1} + e_k (`F-LEDGER-CHAIN-IS-A-SUM-IN-U`), and a commutative sum is precisely the object that does not care what order its terms arrive in. If that commutativity reaches the ENTRIES rather than stopping at the u's, all 719 rearrangements of every ledger are accepted, the count is 1,438,000 rather than 1,972, and the mixer is no better than the sum on the one family the sum cannot see at all. The change of variable is triangular, which is my reason for expecting it not to, and triangularity is doing the entire job -- nothing in `AS` or here has yet evaluated that head on a PERMUTED ledger. Failing low is live too: an adjacent transposition changes exactly two of the u's, so its accept condition is a collision in a SUM OF TWO g-values rather than in one, and if sums of two g-values collide less often than chance the ratio drops under 0.85.
predictions.note: Held on all three legs: 0.9746 of the exact chance expectation, a variance-to-mean ratio of 1.0392, and a worst ledger of 6 against a line at 10. The control is the part that makes it readable and it is not a statistic but a certainty -- the summed head accepts 1,426,480 of 1,426,480 rearrangements, every single one, because the multiset of entries is unchanged. On this family the mixer is the only thing standing, and it stands at exactly chance. The registered route to failure was AS's own D2: this head is a commutative sum of g-values in the reparametrised variable u_k, and a commutative sum does not care about order. It does not transfer, because the change of variable is triangular and a rearrangement changes every u -- had it transferred the count would have been 1,438,000 rather than 1,907. The move sub-family, which is what a verifier that COUNTS entries still faces, is 49,903 distinct length-preserving moves accepted 65 times against a chance of 68.45.

prediction_sets.subject: What does the WIDTH of a ledger head buy a forger, and what does it not? A family of permutation-based heads at widths 1 through 6 trits -- 3 to 729 states, all exhaustively enumerable -- with AS's meet-in-the-middle join and second-preimage scan and AT's insertion and universal-pair attacks re-priced at every width, against exact finite-N nulls computed before the run

predictions.claim: the ops currency is linear in the state count and width buys the forger's memory, not his time: over six widths with 24 random heads each, (a) the mean index of the first accepted compensating forgery divided by the exact finite-family null lies in [0.93, 1.07] at every width from 1 to 6 including width one where no carry exists, (b) the meet-in-the-middle join's yield ratio has a mean within 0.03 of 1.0 at widths 2 to 6 so AS's 6.99 operations per forgery is seven at every width while the table grows as 4N^2, and (c) the split-round head at widths 4 and 6 lies inside the random family's min-to-max range on both statistics
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: width one is the route and I am registering it INSIDE the band rather than outside. At one trit the compensating family collapses -- d runs over two values, F is 30 rather than 10,920, and the tritwise difference EQUALS the arithmetic delta at every entry, so `AS`'s four-cell carry partition (which ran 0.989 to 1.042 times chance at width six) has one cell and the mismatch that every attack in this thread runs against is gone. I have one observation pointing that way and it is about this set's OTHER cost statistic: a 40-head probe of the collision scan at width one, run while building the instrument and recorded below, found 63 of 120 rows with NO collision at all and a mean of 2.000 against an exact null of 2.889 -- a 31% miss. So width one is already known to break one of this set's two cost laws, and (a) predicts it does not break this one. For (b), `AS3`'s registered failure route was that the join's two half-tables might have coinciding key sets, which returns the sum of squared counts rather than the product of means -- 2.0 times ideal, and the tool measures 2.0003 for the degenerate case at width six. That did not fire at 531,441 keys; at width TWO the join has 81 keys and 81 rows a side with about two thirds of the keys occupied, which is where the Poisson approximation behind "the mean is one" is weakest among the widths (b) covers, and a mean ratio past 1.03 at any of widths 2 to 6 refutes it. The responsiveness control is itself width-dependent and that is on the record below: a join whose halves are identical returns 1.0000 at width one, about 1.8 at width two and 2.00 from width three up, so at width two the control's own span is 1.0 to 1.8.
predictions.note: Held on all three legs, and one of them is not evidence and is reported as such. (b) and (c) held with room: the join returns between 0.9933 and 1.0105 of ideal at every width from 2 to 6 and 1.0000 at width one where the left key map is a bijection, so AS's seven operations per forgery is seven operations per forgery at EVERY width and what width actually buys is the 4N^2 table -- 36 slots at width one against 2,125,764 at width six. All 20,199 rebuilt joined forgeries reproduce both heads. The split-round head sits inside the random family's range on both statistics at widths four and six, so the law is about width and not about D's mixer. (a) HELD AT WIDTH TWO BY 0.0002, at 0.9302 against a line at 0.93, and a redraw of the same population at four seeds gives 0.9684, 0.9243, 1.0275 and 0.9693 -- one of the four below the line. THE LEG IS NOT EVIDENCE. T-CRITERION-IN-THE-NOISE, fifth bite, and the first time on a line that PASSED: the four earlier bites were all found because a criterion failed, and a criterion in the noise that happens to pass is the same defect with nothing to make anybody look. The other five widths held with room -- 1.0000, 1.0316, 1.0131, 0.9940 and 0.9637 -- and width one held exactly, for a structural reason no prediction claimed: 4,800 of 4,800 scans at width one return index 3, every time.

predictions.claim: the collision law is the only square root in this thread and it has a floor: (a) the mean first-repeat index divided by the exact birthday null lies in [0.95, 1.06] at widths 4, 5 and 6 with no collision-free row at those widths, (b) the least-squares slope of log mean against log N over widths 2 to 6 lies in [0.45, 0.55] for the collision scan and in [0.95, 1.05] for the second-preimage scan, and (c) the shortfall at the narrow end is a multiplicity effect and not an ordering one -- at widths 1, 2 and 3 the measured mean divided by the mean over 200 random reshuffles of each row's own multiset of head values lies in [0.95, 1.05] at each of the three
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: (a) can fail by the scan being EMPTY, which is not hypothetical. `ladderlang`'s `HASH27.md` measured this exact head shape read one-headed -- h_old(a, b) = P(a + b) - b -- and found the fixed-b orientation has NO COLLISION IN ANY ROW, at 6 trits and again at 162, because that map is a bijection. My row map is x -> STEP[g(x)][c - x], whose first factor is g and therefore not injective at width six, where `AS` measured g's image at 465 of 729; if the image fraction climbs toward 1 as the head narrows the rows go collision-free and (a) fails at width four the way the probe says it already fails at width one. (c) can fail in the other direction: the scan runs x in ASCENDING index order, which is not a random order, and if the head correlates a repeat with small |x| the measured mean falls below the reshuffled one and the ratio drops under 0.95 -- that would be a structural finding rather than a width law, and it is why (c) is registered separately from (a).
predictions.note: FAILED on leg (c) at width one alone, and the reason it fails is the mechanism it was asserting. At width one the measured scan finds no collision in any of 72 rows AND the reshuffled null finds none in any of 14,400 -- the row map is injective, so the multiset has no repeated value and no ordering can produce a collision. The ratio is 0/0. The registration named width one as degenerate in this very statistic's rationale and then included it in (c) anyway; that is the defect, and the sentence as written is not satisfied. (a) and (b) held. The first-repeat index tracks the exact finite-N birthday null to within 0.6% at widths four, five and six -- 1.0057, 1.0017 and 0.9938 -- with zero collision-free rows in 25,272 scanned, and the two slopes come out at 0.4642 and 1.0031 against registered bands at [0.45, 0.55] and [0.95, 1.05]. SO THE TWO ATTACK GOALS SEPARATE BY EXACTLY ONE SQUARE ROOT AND THE SEPARATION IS MEASURED. (c) held at widths two and three, 1.0208 and 1.0492, and the width-three value sits 0.0008 inside its line with a four-seed spread of 1.0492, 1.0034, 1.0320 and 0.9875, so that leg is thin too and is reported as such. The affine control settles the responsiveness: it is collision-free on every row at widths one and two and on one row in nine at widths three, five and six, where its mean first repeat at width six is 84.47 against a null of 34.51 -- 2.45x, so the statistic spans from undefined to well above its null before any subject value is read.

predictions.claim: growth is nearly free of width and length beats width: (a) the mean shortest insertion-only forgery tracks AT's counting null to within 0.30 at every width from 1 to 6, (b) the least-squares slope of log mean against log N over widths 1 to 6 is under 0.32 against 0.5 for the birthday law and 1.0 for AU1's ops law, and (c) the same slope measured at ledger length twelve is at least 0.05 smaller than at length six
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: the counting null assumes the L + 1 forced values are L + 1 independent uniform draws on Z_N, and they are L + 1 reads of ONE bijection -- the forced value at accumulator a is u* (-) a, so DISTINCT GENERATORS ARE EXACTLY DISTINCT ACCUMULATORS VISITED. At width one a seven-gap chain walks three states, so at most three of the seven generators can differ, and at width six seven gaps on 729 states essentially never repeat. `AT2` registered exactly this route -- "a repeated accumulator contributes a DUPLICATE generator rather than a new one" -- and it did not fire at 729; this set runs it at the width where it must be largest. If duplication costs the forger anything the measured mean at width one or two exceeds its null by more than 0.30 and (a) fails at the narrow end, which would also push (b)'s slope down and make (b) hold for the wrong reason. In the other direction (b) fails if the shortfall at the narrow end is so severe that the curve is steeper than a cube root. For (c) the hazard is that at length twelve the null is nearly flat across these widths -- 1.0131 to 3.3521 -- so the slope is small, and a gap of 0.05 between two small slopes is the kind of line `T-CRITERION-IN-THE-NOISE` has fired on four times; the seed-to-seed spread of both slopes is therefore reported beside them and the band is placed at four times the null spread of the difference rather than at a round number.
predictions.note: Held on all three legs. (a) held with room everywhere: the largest gap from AT's counting null over the six widths is 0.0887, at width six, against a registered 0.30 -- so a heuristic that was checked at one width predicts the shortest insertion-only forgery at every width in this sweep, at both ledger lengths. AT2's registered failure route did not fire even where it must be largest: at width one a seven-gap chain visits only 2.822 distinct accumulators of seven, so five of the seven forced generators are duplicates, AND THE DUPLICATION COSTS THE FORGER NOTHING -- 1.064 against a null of 1.097. (b) held at 0.2812. THAT IS THE ANSWER TO THE SET'S OWN QUESTION IN THE GROWTH CURRENCY: five more trits of head multiply the state count by 243 and the growth cost by 4.66. (c) held at a gap of 0.0545 against a line at 0.05, and three further seeds at a quarter of the heads and a quarter of the ledgers give 0.0494, 0.0441 and 0.0597 -- two of the three below the line. That leg is a criterion in the noise and is reported as one; the DIRECTION is stable at every seed (0.2266 against 0.2812 here, and lower at length twelve at all three further seeds) and only the size of the gap is not.

predictions.claim: no width in this sweep extinguishes the zero-operation forgery: over 400 random heads at each of six widths, (a) the measured fraction of heads admitting at least one universal pair lies in [0.56, 0.70] at every width from 2 to 6, (b) that fraction at width 6 is not the smallest of those five, and (c) pooled over heads the measured fraction of accumulators admitting no pair lies in [0.335, 0.395] at every width from 2 to 6 -- a band placed around AT's own measured 0.35117 rather than around the Poisson closed form 0.36788
predictions.at_risk: AT RISK: the accumulator this whole statistic hangs on is DISTINGUISHED, and `AT`'s closing sentence is that gap zero is never a random accumulator. At the tritwise identity the accept condition collapses from a generic equation to P(P(x) (+) x) = -x, a self-composition of the head rather than an independent draw, and a self-composition is exactly the shape whose fixed-point count is not Poisson(1): for a uniform permutation the expected number of fixed points of sigma^2 is 2, not 1. If that excess propagates, (a) fails high at several widths at once. The narrow end is where a distributional claim goes to die -- at width one there are THREE accumulators and three values of x, and a Poisson argument has no business being trusted there, which is why widths 2..6 are the registered range and width one is reported. What I have pointing the other way is one measured total: `AT` reports 741 fixed points summed over the 729 accumulators against a random-permutation control's 735 and a random-function step table's 751, so the excess over N at width six is 12 on a spread of about 27 and is 0.4 standard deviations. That is the arithmetic saying the effect is not there; (a) and (c) are the measurement asking whether it is there at widths nobody has run.
predictions.note: FAILED at width two, on legs (a) and (c) together, and the failure is a property of the head family I chose rather than of width -- which the set can say only because it ran the unconditioned family beside the conditioned one. At width two the conditioned family reads 0.5275 against a band at [0.56, 0.70] and 0.45833 of accumulators admitting none against [0.335, 0.395]; the UNCONDITIONED family at the same width reads 0.6450 and a mean c(ZERO) of 0.965, comfortably where the closed form says. CONDITIONING ON EXACTLY ONE FIXED POINT -- which is what makes a head comparable to D's P and what gives it an insertion family at all -- is what pushes width two out of band, at nine states where one constraint is a ninth of the object. T-CLAIM-NARROWED-BY-A-DESIGN, sixth bite, caught by the control rather than by a reader. (b) held: width six's 0.6450 is not the smallest, width two's 0.5275 is. Widths 3, 4, 5 and 6 all held on both legs -- 0.6075, 0.6625, 0.6000, 0.6450 and 0.35185, 0.37397, 0.35340, 0.35900 -- so from 27 states up the answer is stable and it is the one that matters: ABOUT TWO THIRDS OF HEADS AT EVERY WIDTH ADMIT A TWO-ENTRY, ZERO-OPERATION, ZERO-KNOWLEDGE FORGERY, and width six is not rarer than width three. Width one is the other end of the same degeneracy and is reported rather than registered: every head has exactly one universal pair at every accumulator, so the fraction is 1.0000 and no accumulator admits none.
